newsitem.title: FRANCE: First French election round won't end share risk.
newsitem.headline: First French election round won't end share risk.

text.p: The first round in the French parliamentary election on Sunday is unlikely to remove political risk from the French share market and trading will be volatile until after June 1.

Financial analysts said on Thursday that while the market was assuming the centre-right government coalition would win, it would wait until the second round on June 1 before removing a discount for the political risk that the opposition Socialist party would win with help from the Communist Party.
"The May 25 election is largely irrelevant," said a market strategist at an investment bank in London.
"Only about 10 percent of seats will be decided in the first round and abstentions will be high. It's June 1 which is the real important date," he said.

An illustration of the political risk was provided by Paris Bourse trading on Thursday with the CAC-40 index posting a loss of 1.6 percent at 2,741.86 at 1426 GMT partly due to rumours about unpublished opinion polls.

"The market is down ahead of the close of the market account on Friday after we had a good rise this month with a fresh record high. Talk about opinion polls is also dragging the market down," a broker said.
The CAC-40 reached an all-time high of 2,804.53 on May 16. The index closed at 2,547.56 on Friday April 18 before President Jacques Chirac called the snap election.
Strategist Bryan Allworthy at Merrill Lynch in London said he believed the markets expected a win by the centre-right government coalition, albeit with a smaller majority than at the moment.
Were the government to win there would be a little upswing in the share market and the blue-chip CAC-40 index could rise further to 3,100 at the end of 1997.
Allworthy recently increased his end of year CAC-40 forecast after upping profit forecasts for some companies and a less negative view on bond markets.
He said that if the Socialists won, investors would carefully look at how many Communist ministers would enter government, which ministries they would get and what the government policies would be.
"There could be a three to four percent downward price correction in the first few days and during the rest of the day the market could slip for some 10 percent," he said.

"But even under a Left-wing victory, we do not expect French shares to underperform other European markets," he added, saying that Spanish and Italian equities would be doing relatively worse while German companies would have difficulties coping with a stronger mark as a result of a flight into mark assets.
Jean-Pierre Filbien, a director at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Paris, also warned that the outcome of the May 25 first round was far from decisive.
"We could well be in for some surprises on Monday morning. The vote for the right could be fragmented, absentions could be high," he said.
Filbien added in France voters in general used the first round to express their discontent with government policy and the second to vote for the team they want to see in power.
Ben Funnell, an analyst at Morgan Stanley in London, said the U.S. investment house remained negative on the French stock market even if the government won.
"If the centre-right wins, we see some franc strength on the mark crosses which would permit the Bank of France to cut rates. This would boost economic growth and could help shares," he said.

However, Morgan Stanley maintained its end-1997 target for the CAC-40 of 2,250. "We believe that France and other European markets are overvalued and that there will be a downward correction," he said.
"What we don't know exactly is when it will happen and what will be the trigger," he said.
